lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You flagged Should big cities charge cars to enter downtown? — over to you.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: I drive into the city for work and the new toll would cost me hundreds a month. I think congestion pricing is just a tax on working people.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: That's a very direct point regarding the financial impact on commuters.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, over to you.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Calling it just a tax on working people is the easy way out; the whole point of congestion pricing is to make the *system* work better, not just to raise revenue.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan saying the system needs fixing, and I think that's true, but I also really want to acknowledge the very real strain this puts on people who rely on their car to get to work. It feels like we have to balance the big picture with the immediate reality of people's budgets.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy's right about the immediate reality, but we can't let the fear of the toll paralyze us into keeping the gridlocked status quo.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I understand the desire to move past the status quo, but I wonder if we've fully explored what support systems would need to be in place to make this transition fair for those who can't easily switch to public transit

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, take it away.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy is asking for the safety net, and that's a valid concern, but we can't let the need for perfect implementation stop us from trying to fix the core problem

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, you're up.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I hear your point that we can't let perfect implementation stop us, but I worry that if we rush forward without those supports, we risk making the system feel punitive to the very people who need to get to work. It feels like we need both the ambition for change and the empathy for the people affected by it

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, over to you.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy keeps framing this as a choice between ambition and empathy, but I see it as a failure to design a system that *doesn't* punish people in the first place.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Amy — you're on.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I think the idea of designing a system that doesn't punish people is the ultimate goal, and I agree with that aspiration. But for the people who are already feeling the pinch, like the guest who mentioned the cost, the immediate feeling is that the system *is* punishing them right now
